# `ggplot2`

`ggplot2` builds plots in layers, following the "grammar of graphics."
```{r message=FALSE, fig.height=3, fig.width=8}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

iris %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = Petal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(~Species) +
  theme_minimal()
```

For a full systematic introduction to `ggplot2`, see the
[Data Visualization chapters of R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize.html)
or [this ggplot2 bookdown guide](https://bookdown.org/ozancanozdemir/introduction-to-ggplot2/).

# `plotly`

`plotly` turns static plots into interactive, hover-able ones:
```{r message=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
library(plotly)

plot_ly(data = iris %>% count(Species),
        labels = ~Species, values = ~n, type = "pie")
```

`ggpubr::ggpie()` gives a similar publication-ready pie chart built on
`ggplot2`:
```{r message=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
library(ggpubr)

ggpie(data = iris %>% count(Species) %>%
        mutate(label = paste0(Species, " (", round(100 * n / sum(n), 2), "%)")),
      x = "n", label = "label", color = "white",
      fill = "Species", lab.pos = "in")
```

See the [plotly R docs](https://plotly.com/r/) and
[this intro-to-DS plotting chapter](https://bookdown.org/ronsarafian/IntrotoDS/plotting.html)
for more.
